newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Rivlin says over-heating is economic threat.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Rivlin says over-heating is economic threat.

text.p: U.S. Federal Reserve Board Vice Chairman Alice Rivlin said on Monday that the major threat to the U.S. economy at the moment was the possibility of over-heating.
"The major threat at the moment is not that the economy will run out of steam (but) that's always possible," Rivlin said in a speech to the Employment Policy Foundation.
"The thing that worries the federal reserve more is the possible overheating of the economy," she added.
Rivlin said that the economy was quite strong across the United States, and that labor markets were uniformly tight, which she said had brought a number of benefits.
"To be sure we have not seen the rising prices that we might have expected at this stage of the business cycle," she said.

"But what we are seeing is high consumer demand, the beginnings of wage increases, which can only be good, and the possibility that those wage increases will be passed along in price increases if the economy keeps going at its current pace," she added.
She said the challenge to everybody, including the Federal Reserve, was how to keep the growth and the tight labor markets going without running into difficulties.

She repeated that the recent Fed rate hike was a "small insurance policy to say that we were concerned about the over-rapid growth of the economy and the chance that we might blow this good opportunity by having inflation accelerate down the road, six months to a year from now."
She said that what the Fed did next would depend on how upcoming economic statistics turned out.
"We at the Federal Reserve will continue to watch and monitor," Rivlin said.
She described it as a "stitch-in-time" process, but that it was difficult to know when exactly a stitch would be necessary.

Rivlin also called for more political effort to keep the budget deficit from rising. And she said that the productivity of the U.S. economy was not being measured very well and was probably underestimated.
"There's every reason to think we're doing better than we think we are," she said of productivity.
Rivlin suggested a temporary fix to the consumer price index that could be put in place while the Bureau of Labor Statistics was given additional resources to work on correcting the measure.
A commision headed by Stanford University Economist Michael Boskin report last year that the CPI overstated inflation by 1.1 percentage points a year.
Rivlin suggested a political agreement to discount the CPI by 0.4 of a percentage point for up to five years while the changes were made.
"I would pick a much smaller number like 0.4 so almost no one could say it was an overestimate of the overestimate and legislate a temporary reduction in the index," she said.

"I would give the bureau of labor statistics additional resources, considerable additional resources...and a strong mandate to improve the index as much as they can and particularly to focus on question of the changing quality of products."
Rivlin acknowledged that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan had suggested another commission to decide on the appropriate discount to the CPI.
"I just don't think you need it, I think the politicians could sit down and agree on some number which would be quite arbitrary and that's all the commission could do either," she said.
Rivlin said there were certainly wage increases being seen in the economy but they had been slower than expected.
"It hasn't been especially rapid. I think most economists would have predicted more wage increases at these tight labor markets than we've gotten."
Rivlin also said the stability of inflation despite rising wages was surprising but tended to reinforce the idea that productivity was higher than the data suggested.
